verses.1: Al-Mizan reads al-najm as any luminous heavenly body and its setting as descent toward the western horizon, rejecting readings of it as the Qurʾan, the Pleiades, Sirius, or a shooting star because the wording supports none of them. It takes ‘your companion’ to mean the Messenger and distinguishes ḍalāl, straying from the right path, from ghayy, error arising from false belief or opinion. The verse thus denies that he erred either about human felicity through serving God or about the path that attains it.

verses.3: Al-Mizan limits the denial that the Prophet speaks from hawā, the ego’s desire and opinions, to his call to God and recitation of the Qurʾan, since the context answers idolaters who accused him of fabricating revelation; this speech is revelation from God. It reads ‘taught him’ as able to refer to the Prophet, the Qurʾan, or all revelation, with the object left implicit, and reports that the powerful teacher is read either as Gabriel or as God. It records interpretations of dhū mirra as severity for God, sound intellect, or traversal, applied by commentators to Gabriel and alternatively to the Prophet. Likewise, istiwāʾ may mean standing or exercising authority: Gabriel may have appeared in his created form—reports say only twice—or administered his charge, while a reading referring to the Prophet makes him steadfast. The highest horizon is the loftiest heavenly horizon, not specifically the east, and its pronoun may refer to either Gabriel or the Prophet.

verses.8: Al-Mizan explains danā as drawing near and tadallā as figurative extreme nearness, though the latter has also been connected with hanging or descending. If the pronouns refer to Gabriel, he approached the Prophet, perhaps descending from the highest horizon to take him heavenward; if they refer to the Prophet, he drew increasingly near to God. Qāb qawsayn denotes the measure of two bows or two cubits, or less, and the commentary rejects a proposed reversal of the phrase because it would add no difference in meaning. It canvasses several allocations of the pronouns in the revelation of verse 10—Gabriel revealing to the Prophet, God revealing through Gabriel, or Gabriel conveying what God revealed—but judges the reading in which the preceding pronouns refer to the Prophet and God reveals to His servant to make better sense.

verses.11: Al-Mizan takes kadhaba, when joined to the heart, in the sense of perceptual error: the Prophet’s heart did not err or deceive him in what it saw. The heart, al-fuʾād, can have an interior intuitive vision distinct from the external senses, imagination, and discursive thought; it also perceives one’s perceptions themselves. The immediate objects of this vision are the highest horizon, drawing near, and revelation—signs of God—and the verse need not say that God appeared to the Prophet. If it was a vision of God, the commentary says it was a vision of the heart, unlike physical sight, which cannot perceive Him. It rejects readings in which the heart merely confirmed what the Prophet’s eyes saw, including the doubled kadhdhaba recitation, because they would make the Qurʾan establish his vision by his own inward belief. The following dispute is instead a rebuke: people cannot meaningfully debate with one who reports something directly witnessed.
verses.12: Al-Mizan treats the question about disputing the Prophet’s vision as a rhetorical rebuke: the idolaters persist in contesting what he directly experienced. Nazla ordinarily means a descent. One interpretation says the Prophet saw Gabriel in his original form at the Lote Tree after Gabriel descended to take him heavenward; the commentary instead considers it more apparent, from its earlier discussion, that the Prophet was set down at the Lote Tree during his ascent and there again saw God with his heart. Sidrat al-muntahā is a known Lote tree at a specific, perhaps utmost heavenly, boundary; its description and what covered it are deliberately left ambiguous. A reported explanation places it above the Seven Heavens, where human deeds are delivered. The nearby Garden of the Abode is read as the limited, temporary paradise of Barzakh for the faithful, distinct from final paradise.

verses.17: Al-Mizan glosses zāgh as inclining from uprightness and taghā as exceeding the limits. The Prophet’s gaze neither perceived what it saw other than as it was nor perceived anything unreal; it was flawless. This is the vision of his heart, not his eyes, at the later vision, and it indicates an earlier similar heart-vision as well.
verses.18: Al-Mizan reads the Prophet’s sight of some of his Lord’s greatest signs as witnessing God through the heart by witnessing His signs as signs, for every sign points beyond itself to its referent. It distinguishes this from seeing God’s essence without the mediation of signs or piercing the divine veil, which it holds impossible (20:11).
verses.19: Al-Mizan turns from the confirmed truth of the Prophet’s revelation to tawḥīd, which logically excludes partners from God. The mention of Lāt, ʿUzza, and Manāt begins a refutation of their divinity, lordship, supposed femininity, and independent power of intercession, as well as the idolaters’ claims about angels and the Resurrection. Because reports about these three idols’ forms, locations, worshippers, and origins conflict and cannot be verified, the commentary confines itself to what is certain. The verses ask the idolaters to account for these alleged angels or daughters of God in light of the established truth of the Prophet’s mission.

verses.21: Al-Mizan takes the question as a rhetorical denial tinged with derision: if the angelic spirits of the idols are alleged to be God’s daughters while the idolaters prefer sons for themselves, assigning males to themselves and females to God is, by their own terms, an unjust division.

verses.23: Al-Mizan says that Lāt, ʿUzza, Manāt, or idols generally are merely names coined by the idolaters and their fathers, without a reality to which their alleged divinity refers or any sulṭān, proof, from God. Their beliefs follow conjecture and the soul’s selfish inclinations despite the guidance brought by their true Lord through the Messenger or the Qurʾan. The shift from directly addressing them to speaking of them in the third person implies that they are not prepared to hear decisive arguments while they remain attached to conjecture and desire.
verses.24: Al-Mizan reads the question as denying that a person obtains whatever he desires. The idolaters have no proof that their idols are divinities or that angels may independently intercede; they want those claims to be true, but wishing does not make them true.
verses.25: Al-Mizan presents God’s exclusive possession of this world and the Hereafter as the reason human beings cannot have whatever they wish: both realms belong to Him alone, without a partner in His dominion.
verses.26: Al-Mizan distinguishes idhn, permission that removes an impediment, from riḍā, approval of what pleases the approver: approval entails permission, but permission need not entail approval. The verse rejects the idolaters’ claim that angels intercede independently of God; intercession is possible only after He permits it and approves it. ‘Whomever He wishes’ may refer to the angels, so only approved angels may intercede, or to human beings, in which case God would not approve or permit intercession for one who disbelieves and worships other deities.
verses.27: Al-Mizan repudiates the idolaters’ claim that angels are God’s daughters: giving female names to angels means treating the angelic species as feminine, not merely giving one or more angels female names. It reports an alternative that they named each angel a daughter of God, and another explanation that links this act with disbelief in the Hereafter because only one who disbelieves in it would dare an act so grave.
verses.28: Al-Mizan defines ʿilm as an undeniably true belief, ẓann as the more likely of two possibilities, and wahm as the less likely. The idolaters’ belief that angels are feminine has no basis even for likelihood; because selfish inclination makes them ignore contrary indications and cling to what they desire, the Qurʾan calls their fantasy ẓann. This also supports reading ẓann in (53:23) as imagination rather than probable belief. Ḥaqq is reality as it is, and the commentary says the verse appears to make knowledge its only sure basis; beliefs that admit their opposites cannot establish doctrine. Acting on conjecture in practical Islamic rulings is allowed only where evidence qualifies this principle.
verses.29: Al-Mizan explains that the command to avoid them identifies its reason by calling them those who turn from God’s remembrance: they abandon knowledge for conjecture and selfish desire because they want only worldly life. Dhikrinā may mean the Qurʾan, which leads through decisive proofs to truth and eternal felicity, or remembrance of God through His names and attributes, which discloses the realities of the Origin and the Return. Their worldliness is therefore the limit of their knowledge, and the Prophet is commanded to keep apart from their error.
verses.30: Al-Mizan takes ‘that’ to refer to worldly life: it is the mablagh, the furthest point their knowledge reaches, so it becomes the whole object of their desire, ambition, and hope. God’s knowledge of those who stray and those who are guided reinforces this judgment as His testimony to it.
verses.31: Al-Mizan offers two connected readings. God’s ownership of all that is in the heavens and earth may qualify His perfect knowledge of the guided and astray, and the requital clause may continue the command to leave the idolaters to Him. More apparently, the verse is a new statement: leaving them does not mean they are neglected, for Allah’s explicit name stresses His greatness and His complete dominion, creation, and governance. The purpose of this dominion is requital in the Hereafter: evil and good are disobedience and obedience, and bi mā ʿamilū may mean recompense for deeds or with their reality. Thus those who disobey receive their due, while those who obey receive the best reward.
verses.32: Al-Mizan defines kabāʾir al-ithm as major sins—an Imām al-Bāqir narration identifies them as sins threatened with hellfire—and fawāḥish as abominable sins, including fornication and sodomy, apparently among the major sins. It records readings of lamam as minor sins, acts leading to sin, or occasional, unhabituated slips; traditions of the Prophet’s Household support the last reading, including reports from Imām al-Ṣādiq that a person slips into a sin and seeks forgiveness or returns to it without making it his nature. The doers of good therefore avoid major sins and indecencies while still having lapses, and God’s expansive forgiveness invites repentance. His bringing people forth in stages from the earth and knowing them as fetuses means He knows their reality, secrets, and outcome from their beginning; they must not proclaim themselves pure, since He knows the Godwary best.
verses.33: Al-Mizan reads the verses, in light of what follows, as asking about a man who turned away from spending in God’s way, gave only a little of his wealth, and then akdā, stopped spending altogether. The opening fa connects this example to the preceding exposition.
verses.34: Al-Mizan reads the verses, in light of what follows, as asking about a man who turned away from spending in God’s way, gave only a little of his wealth, and then akdā, stopped spending altogether. The opening fa connects this example to the preceding exposition.
verses.35: Al-Mizan takes the question as a rhetorical denial that the man who stopped spending knows the Unseen. Some explain this as a denial that he knows a companion will bear his sins and punishment; the commentary considers it more fitting that he cannot know his future well enough to be certain continued spending will exhaust his wealth and bring poverty. The question of another bearing his burden is addressed separately in the following verse.
verses.36: Al-Mizan identifies the scriptures of Moses as the Torah and Abraham’s scriptures as what God sent him, while Abraham’s ‘fulfilling’ means that he rendered divine servanthood in its fullest measure. The ensuing aphoristic teachings confront the man who withheld spending: no wāzira bears another’s wizr, so no soul is sinful or punished for another’s deed. What innately belongs to a person, al-mulk al-ḥaqīqī, is only the good or evil he earns by his acts; wealth, children, and status are temporary social possessions left behind at death. Intercession for grave sinners, posthumous prayers and gifted rewards do not contradict this, because they result from the recipient’s faithful effort, membership in and support for the community of faith. Likewise, one who institutes a sunna ḥasana receives the reward of those who follow it, while an originator of evil bears their burden, because his effort contributed to their actions. Each person will be shown his endeavour on the Resurrection—the passive wording suggests others also see it—and receive a wholly complete reward. Muntahā means every end without restriction: all beings, their effects, and cosmic governance begin with and ultimately devolve to God, returning to Him through the Resurrection; readings that limit it to return, reward and punishment, judgment, or the limits of thought lack textual warrant. The subsequent exclusive acts exemplify this lordship. Intermediate physical and metaphysical causes operate only under God’s will, while a human act belongs to its chooser as well as to God as ultimate originator; divine will concerns the chosen act as chosen, avoiding both the jābira’s denial of human agency and the Muʿtazila’s separation of it from God. The same applies to death and life. Nuṭfa is the seed of man and woman from which the male and female mates are created; the altered wording may underscore that no other can create them. The second genesis is God’s irrevocable promised new creation for recompense. Aghnā is granting wealth and aqnā lasting possessions, though alternative readings make the latter contentment or impoverishment. Sirius is a bright eastern star; reports connect its worship to Khuzāʿa, Ḥimyar, and Abū Kabsha. The former ʿĀd are Hūd’s people, distinguished from a later people of that name; Thamūd’s unbelievers were destroyed while the faithful were saved. Noah’s people were more unjust and rebellious because few answered his long call. The overturned town may be Lot’s people or, more generally, any punished town left in ruin.

Intermediate physical and metaphysical causes operate only under God’s will, while a human act belongs to its chooser as well as to God as ultimate originator; divine will concerns the chosen act as chosen, avoiding both the jābira’s denial of human agency and the Muʿtazila’s separation of it from God. The same applies to death and life. Nuṭfa is the seed of man and woman from which the male and female mates are created; the altered wording may underscore that no other can create them. The second genesis is God’s irrevocable promised new creation for recompense. Aghnā is granting wealth and aqnā lasting possessions, though alternative readings make the latter contentment or impoverishment. Sirius is a bright eastern star; reports connect its worship to Khuzāʿa, Ḥimyar, and Abū Kabsha. The former ʿĀd are Hūd’s people, distinguished from a later people of that name; Thamūd’s unbelievers were destroyed while the faithful were saved. Noah’s people were more unjust and rebellious because few answered his long call. The overturned town may be Lot’s people or, more generally, any punished town left in ruin.
verses.54: Al-Mizan identifies the scriptures of Moses as the Torah and Abraham’s scriptures as what God sent him, while Abraham’s ‘fulfilling’ means that he rendered divine servanthood in its fullest measure. The ensuing aphoristic teachings confront the man who withheld spending: no wāzira bears another’s wizr, so no soul is sinful or punished for another’s deed. What innately belongs to a person, al-mulk al-ḥaqīqī, is only the good or evil he earns by his acts; wealth, children, and status are temporary social possessions left behind at death. Intercession for grave sinners, posthumous prayers and gifted rewards do not contradict this, because they result from the recipient’s faithful effort, membership in and support for the community of faith. Likewise, one who institutes a sunna ḥasana receives the reward of those who follow it, while an originator of evil bears their burden, because his effort contributed to their actions. Each person will be shown his endeavour on the Resurrection—the passive wording suggests others also see it—and receive a wholly complete reward. verses.55: Al-Mizan defines ālāʾ as bounties and tatamārī as doubting or disputing, and reads the question as a rhetorical denial concluding the description of God’s cosmic acts. Laughter and tears, death, destruction, and creation are all counted among His blessings because each serves the world’s perfect order, the flourishing of creation, and the return of all things to God. The address may be to the man who withheld spending or, if to the Prophet, indirectly to those around him.
verses.56: Al-Mizan notes that nadhīr may mean ‘warning’ and nudhur may be the plural of either sense; the verse may therefore identify either the Qurʾan or the Prophet as a warner like those of old.
verses.57: Al-Mizan identifies al-Āzifa, ‘the Imminent,’ as a name of the Resurrection and reads its nearness as its soon occurrence.
verses.58: Al-Mizan takes kāshifa to mean alleviating the Resurrection’s terrors and hardships; no soul can relieve them except Allah.
verses.59: Al-Mizan identifies the discourse as the preceding exposition and sāmidūn as the heedless, from samūd, diversion. The rhetorical question rebukes those who, though all matters end with God, the new creation depends on Him, and only He can alleviate the imminent Resurrection, meet the call to salvation with astonishment, denial, and mocking laughter rather than weeping for lost blessings and their exposure to eternal misery.

verses.62: Al-Mizan presents prostration and worship as the final conclusion: since only God can relieve what the coming event contains, people should bow before and worship Him in hope of that relief.
